brief.question: What does the parliamentary record show about housing?
brief.answer:
The most decision-relevant recent finding in the record is the National Housing Finance and Investment Corporation’s State of the nation's housing 2022-23 report, cited by a Labor minister as confirming the need for all government, industry and housing stakeholders to work together and as showing that the proposed Housing Australia Future Fund would double the number of new social housing dwellings added to stock each year for at least the five years from 2024, compared with the period 2006 to 2021. The minister described the fund as a $10 billion fund in legislation before the parliament and insisted the government was determined to pass it, saying too many Australians, particularly vulnerable Australians, were struggling to secure safe and affordable housing.

The record also contains sharp contradictions between promises and delivery. In an earlier exchange, a minister claimed a proud housing record, pointing to a $6 billion investment in social housing that had delivered some 21,000 social housing homes and a $4.5 billion National Rental Affordability Scheme providing incentives to build 50,000 affordable rental homes. A supplementary question immediately challenged that claim, noting that only 10,671 dwellings had been allocated under the National Rental Affordability Scheme over the previous four years against a government target of 50,000 dwellings by June 2016, and asking when the remaining 35,000-plus would be delivered. Later, another minister defended the Gillard-era record by citing 14,500 social housing units complete, 80,000 premises repaired, 31,000 families benefiting, and more than 3,500 National Rental Affordability Scheme units complete out of 50,000 total, alongside 15,000 jobs for tradespeople.

The debate has shifted from stimulus-era optimism to competing crisis narratives. A 2009-era contribution described the stimulus as working, with housing finance rising 3.6 per cent in April and 13.5 per cent over the year, loans for construction of new owner-occupied homes at their highest since January 2002, and first-home buyer loans at record levels, representing 28 per cent of new loans financed. More recently, Labor speakers have described a housing crisis a generation in the making, inherited after a decade of waste and neglect, with construction costs rising at 17 per cent, the highest rate in half a century, new builds down, and coalition governments that “didn’t even bother to have a housing minister.” Coalition speakers counter that Labor has presided over a massive surge in population growth and a collapse in completions, claiming the coalition averaged 200,000 houses per year while the record is down to 170,000 after three years of Labor, and that “great, $40 billion on housing for fewer houses” than the previous government built.

The sharpest disagreements are over who blocked supply and whether announced funding was real. Labor figures accused the Greens of blocking housing supply and the Liberals of past cuts, while the Greens criticised overdevelopment and a lack of political will on urban policy, opposed projects like WestConnex, and advocated for affordable housing. One speaker accused the government of abolishing the Major Cities Unit, failing to appoint a minister for housing, issuing no national urban policy, and presenting a $75 billion infrastructure package as a sham, with only $24.3 billion actually funded and Commonwealth infrastructure grants projected to fall from 0.4 to 0.2 per cent of GDP. State Labor MPs defended their records with specific figures, including the $5.3 billion Big Housing Build with 7,600 homes completed or underway, a $1 billion regional fund, and $232.7 million in extra public housing funding to deliver 564 new homes, while pointing to Liberal governments that reduced public housing by 13,000 properties in earlier decades.

On promises versus reported outcomes, the most direct mismatches are the National Rental Affordability Scheme target compared with allocations, and the gap between the Coalition’s claim of a $75 billion infrastructure package and the $24.3 billion the speaker said was actually funded. There is also a direct personal clash recorded: “I was the housing minister and I passed these laws,” said one member; “You are the housing minister and you have delayed them.” The record repeatedly shows housing framed as a crisis requiring urgent legislative action, whether through the $10 billion Housing Australia Future Fund or state tenancy reforms, but with each side citing different baselines to claim either progress or failure.

sections.question: What have MPs said about housing affordability and home ownership?
sections.answer:
MPs across parties agree housing affordability is a serious national issue, but they sharply diverge on causes and solutions.

**Labor and crossbench critics** argue the crisis is driven by policy failures, especially tax concessions. They cite falling home ownership—from 68–70% (1971–2001) to below 50% by 2017, and a 60-year low—and note that for 25–34 year olds, ownership dropped from 60% to under 40% in 30 years. They point to investor activity and negative gearing as key drivers, with landlord tax losses growing from a $700 million profit in 1998–99 to a $7.8 billion loss in 2010–11. They criticise the government for rejecting Labor’s proposed changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax, and for measures like the foreign resident capital gains withholding increase (10% to 12.5%, threshold lowered from $2 million to $750,000) as inadequate. They also oppose early access to superannuation for housing as regressive and ineffective, and highlight that first-home buyers in Sydney need 40 years of savings for a deposit.

**Coalition speakers** defend the government’s record, arguing that home ownership is high—around 70%—and that affordability is best improved by keeping unemployment low, real wages rising, interest rates low, and ensuring land release and efficient construction. They reject claims of a crisis, noting that housing affordability in the 1990s and under the coalition was stronger than under Labor in the 1980s. They support lateral ideas like the Menzies Foundation concept and argue that government interference limiting land supply has driven up prices, costing 900,000 Australians the chance to own a home. They call for releasing more land, moving departments to regional centres, and reducing stamp duty.

**A crossbench MP** proposed a nuanced approach: expanding the Reserve Bank’s duty to include housing affordability, reviewing negative gearing, using superannuation for homebuyers, and introducing owner-occupier deductibility and a home hedge fund. Another criticised both major parties for abandoning evidence-based policy, proposing investor-driven inflation controls and strategic decentralisation while opposing scrapping negative gearing.

**One speaker** highlighted the role of bipartisan inquiries, noting that home ownership fell from over 70% in the early 1970s to a 60-year low, and warned that within 10 years less than 50% of Australians will own their home. They called on leaders to set aside politics and work together on spreading wealth and stabilising families through home ownership.

sections.question: What positions have been taken on negative gearing and property tax concessions?
sections.answer:
Labor’s current policy, set to start 1 July 2027, restricts negative gearing to newly built residential properties and halves the capital gains tax discount, aiming to help first-home buyers and boost housing supply. Supporters argue these concessions overwhelmingly benefit wealthier Australians—over 50% of negative gearing benefits go to the top 20% of earners—and distort investment away from productive uses. The Greens and some economists, including via a Senate motion, have backed reform, citing rising house prices from six times young income in 1990 to twelve times in 2013.

Opponents, including the Coalition and some crossbench voices, call negative gearing “income tax 101,” standard practice for over 1.4 million Australians, and warn Labor’s changes would crash property prices, destabilise rental markets, and hurt mums and dads, nurses, and teachers—not just wealthy investors. They also point to internal Labor inconsistency: the Leader of the Opposition said in 2023 that negative gearing changes were “not on our radar,” while a Labor frontbencher later claimed the policy had been 18 months in the making. The Coalition instead favours targeted measures like removing travel deductions and imposing vacancy charges on foreign-owned empty properties, while rejecting broad negative gearing or capital gains changes.

sections.question: What has parliament said about social and public housing supply?
sections.answer:
Parliamentary debate shows broad agreement that social and public housing supply is inadequate, but sharp disagreement over the cause and the solution.

Government speakers, including Minister Wong and others, argued that supply is the key driver of housing affordability and rental stress. They pointed to the $32 billion Homes for Australia plan and a target of 55,000 new social and affordable homes over five years, contrasting this with the previous coalition government's record of building only 373 social and affordable homes in nine years. A government representative also noted that over 5,000 of those 55,000 homes were already complete, with 25,000 in planning or construction.

Opposition and crossbench speakers countered that the government's delivery is far too small relative to need. One senator noted that around 190,000 households are on the public housing waitlist, while the government's plan supports at most 55,000 households over 25 years, arguing the scale of delivery does not match demand. Another speaker cited figures of 148,000 on public housing waiting lists and 40,000 on community housing waiting lists, alongside $7.6 billion in Commonwealth housing expenditure in 2016-17.

Specific state-level criticisms were also raised. Rod Roberts highlighted that in South Australia, between 2016 and 2021, the government added 2,257 social housing dwellings but disposed of 3,269, a net loss of over 1,012 dwellings, while nearly 50,000 people remained on the waiting list. Sonia Hornery cited a Compass Housing report showing 48,000 households on the New South Wales waiting list and 175,904 eligible, criticising the government's Future Directions policy for proposing fewer dwellings than half the current waiting list over a decade.

A speaker from the Barwon region urged the Minister for Housing to increase public housing supply, noting 7,101 households on the priority waitlist and that only 72 of 400 planned dwellings at the Commonwealth Games village site were for social and affordable housing. They argued the market has failed, pointing to a decline in public housing from 22% of new housing in 1956 to less than 2% now.

Other speakers called for redirecting tax concessions like negative gearing and capital gains discounts—costing billions annually—to affordable housing, citing reports from Anglicare and the Grattan Institute on rental stress and falling homeownership. One speaker supported a documents motion on planning reforms, noting the New South Wales parliamentary research service found no clear local evidence for government claims that changes would improve affordability or supply.

sections.question: What has parliament said about Housing Supply?
sections.answer:
Parliamentary debate and committee estimates show broad agreement that housing supply is central to affordability, though speakers differ sharply on causes and remedies. A government minister stated: "action on supply is critical, and more supply means better affordability," and defended the $32 billion Homes for Australia plan as "focused on supply, because that is the key." Another minister claimed the budget is "a pro-supply budget," citing an expected "extra 75,000 first home buyers" and that negative gearing "will still be available for new builds." A departmental official in the Social Services portfolio said "ultimately, supply—notwithstanding that that might take some time—is the key driver of keeping down rental stress and improving housing affordability."

Coalition and crossbench speakers challenged the government's record. Senator Hume asked whether the Productivity Commission had assessed the claim that "limiting negative gearing to new builds will support housing supply." Another senator criticised demand-side measures as "bandaids" and argued the government must "better understand what is holding back the supply, by talking to builders, developers and tradespeople." A senator also claimed the government's own tax changes "will decrease supply," while a minister rejected that, saying overall supply would increase over the decade. One speaker accused One Nation and the coalition of voting "to delay the government's Help to Buy housing scheme bill," and another minister said Senator Bragg and the Greens "blocked housing supply" for so long. A senator also referenced the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council's model, noting it projected a supply deficit under baseline population growth but a surplus if growth were 15 per cent less, and questioned why Home Affairs did not collaborate more closely with that council.

sections.question: What has parliament said about the Environmental Planning and Assessment Amendment (Planning System Reforms) Bill 2025?
sections.answer:
The Environmental Planning and Assessment Amendment (Planning System Reforms) Bill 2025, debated in the New South Wales Parliament, drew sharply divided reactions. Government MPs and the Minister for Planning and Public Spaces, Paul Scully (Labor), championed it as a necessary overhaul of a system that has become "weighed down by outdated processes, duplication and inefficiency." They cited broad community support, including from the Planning Institute of Australia, the Master Builders Association, and the Urban Taskforce, with Minister Scully noting an "almost universally positive response" to its passage. Supporters like Dr Marjorie O'Neill (Labor) and Clayton Barr (Labor) argued it would modernise the system, boost housing supply, and remove duplication, with Barr describing it as "the most comprehensive overhaul of our planning system in 50 years." The Opposition also indicated it would support the bill, with Richie Williamson (Nationals) stating the Opposition is "pro-housing, pro-reform" and would work constructively, while moving some amendments.

However, The Greens and other critics strongly opposed the bill. Sue Higginson (Greens) argued it "centralises powers in the hands of the Minister," removes checks and balances, and weakens environmental and community protections, claiming it "replaces an accountable and participatory planning system with one that centralises powers." Kobi Shetty (Greens) called it "a gift for developers" that would not fix the housing crisis but would create corruption risks and gut environmental protections. Dr Amanda Cohn (Greens) echoed these concerns, stating the bill "plainly is not about housing" but about "centralising power and creating opportunities for massive developer profits and corruption." Critics also alleged the Government misrepresented the extent of consultation with the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC), with Higginson claiming ICAC "confirmed that it was not asked to comment on the bill" and that its advice was only general in nature. The Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party supported the bill in principle but expressed concerns it could be used to fast-track projects like mines, while the Libertarian Party supported it as a step towards supply-side reform.

sections.question: What has parliament said about Planning policy and housing?
sections.answer:
Planning policy and housing were discussed in several parliaments. In the New South Wales Parliament, Labor Minister for Planning and Public Spaces Paul Scully said his government inherited a planning system that was "as confused as it was confusing," with a forecast of only 180,000 homes over five years, less than half the requirement under the National Housing Accord. He claimed reforms have cut average development application assessment times by a third, lifted approvals by 27 per cent, and left New South Wales with more than 75,000 homes under construction, the highest in the country. Scully also cited "the biggest rezoning in New South Wales history," a record injection for social housing, and reforms to speed up over 90 per cent of development activity, saying the system should change "from no to yes."

In the same parliament, an opposition member criticised the Victorian Government's housing statement, arguing it had not met targets and that no precinct structure plans had been approved, with no new CBD residential towers announced in Melbourne. In the Commonwealth Parliament, a Labor minister said the government's "Homes for Australia" plan would help 75,000 Australians into home ownership, while a senator from the opposition described the government's housing policy as "the definition of insanity," citing spending and immigration. Another Commonwealth Labor speaker criticised the Coalition's approach, quoting the shadow minister for housing as saying, "We've been too busy talking about the internals of the Liberal Party to do any work." The record also notes a New South Wales ePetition regarding low- and mid-rise housing provisions in Ku-ring-gai, and a question to the Victorian Minister for Planning about Gisborne and Romsey structure plans allegedly sitting on her desk for two years.

sections.question: What has parliament said about Energy policy and housing?
sections.answer:
Parliamentary debate links energy policy and housing mainly through electrification and cost-of-living measures. In the Commonwealth parliament, a government minister said the government is "not supportive of banning new gas connections, because households should have choice," while noting it supports electrification through incentives like the Energy Savings Scheme and the Consumer Energy Strategy. The same minister claimed that houses built to New South Wales' seven-star thermal standard would save households approximately $1,070 per year on energy bills, leaving people "about $700 a year better off." A coalition speaker criticised Labor's energy policy as unachievable, saying "82 per cent renewables—ain't gonna happen!" and accused the government of "legislat[ing] ambition without resourcing it" in both housing and energy.

In the New South Wales parliament, Greens member Abigail Boyd moved a motion congratulating the Victorian Labor Government, the ACT Government and various NSW councils for mandating electrification, and called on the government to "ban new gas connections for residential and commercial developments." She cited the 2024 Net Zero Commission report finding that NSW "is not on track to meet emission reduction targets" and that the built environment sector "is the worst performer, having nearly doubled greenhouse gas emissions between 2005 and 2022." She also referenced Energy Efficiency Council analysis that electrification of Victoria's buildings could free up "an average of 80 petajoules a year through to 2035" for industry.

On housing more broadly, a Commonwealth minister said housing "is going to be an absolutely foremost priority of our government in this second term," and that the government has moved "from being a negligent bystander to one of the most—in fact, the most—active and engaged governments we've seen in the post-war years." The same speaker criticised coalition figures, recalling that Malcolm Turnbull suggested parents should help their kids buy homes and Joe Hockey advised young people to "get a good job that pays good money." A coalition speaker countered that the government "has no answers" and claimed the coalition has announced it is "against Labor's housing policy" and "against Labor's energy policy."

sections.question: What has parliament said about the Strata Schemes Legislation Amendment Bill 2024?
sections.answer:
The New South Wales Legislative Assembly debated the Strata Schemes Legislation Amendment Bill 2024, which implements 37 recommendations from the 2021 statutory review of strata laws. Labor members spoke in support. Ms Julia Finn (Granville) said the bill aims to "enhance transparency, accountability and the overall functioning of strata schemes," covering over 86,000 schemes and more than 40,000 residents in her electorate. She highlighted reforms to prohibit unfair contract terms, require written reasons for refusing minor renovation requests, and address embedded networks. Mr Edmond Atalla (Mount Druitt) called it "a significant step towards ensuring that strata living in New South Wales is safe, affordable and reliable." Ms Jodie Harrison (Charlestown) said it makes strata living fairer for the 1.2 million people in schemes across the State. Ms Charishma Kaliyanda (Liverpool) noted the bill responds to "growing community concerns about practices in the strata professional services sector." Ms Maryanne Stuart (Heathcote) said constituents had been "made to feel fearful by their strata manager" and welcomed the changes as "a respite from the negligence and malpractice that some agents have been able to get away with."

Minister Anoulack Chanthivong (Macquarie Fields), in reply, said the bill "introduces the most significant reforms to strata living and strata laws since 2015." He noted the Government had implemented 31 recommendations in December 2023, passed the Strata Managing Agents Legislation Amendment Act 2024 in September 2024, and that this bill implements a further 37 recommendations, with 36 remaining. Minister Jihad Dib (Bankstown) said the bill's embedded network disclosure changes give "the consumer, the customer, the person who is making the biggest investment of their life, a little more control and understanding." Ms Kylie Wilkinson (East Hills) highlighted reforms on environmental sustainability, financial viability and accessibility, including lowering voting thresholds for accessibility infrastructure to a majority vote. Ms Stephanie Di Pasqua (Drummoyne) said the bill "will go some way to improving the many issues that are experienced by owners in strata schemes."

The Greens were critical. Ms Jenny Leong (Newtown) said the bill "fails to grapple with the regulatory loopholes" around strata agents and that requiring disclosure of embedded networks "is not the same as outlawing that dodgy or less than ideal thing." She also said the bill "does nothing to expand the rights of renters." Ms Cate Faehrmann, in the Legislative Council, said the bill "marks the third tranche of strata reform" and that "the elephant in the room remains: Strata managers continue to receive commissions from insurance companies," advocating for "a complete ban on insurance commissions."

sections.question: What have MPs said about housing affordability and home ownership since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Several MPs addressed housing affordability and home ownership. In the Commonwealth Parliament, a Labor speaker said the government is "addressing housing from every angle: supply, affordability and opportunity," and that in South Australia "that action is now underway." A Labor senator also noted the five per cent deposit scheme "has already helped more than 1,800 Territorians move into their first home" since the government came to office. A Labor MP criticised the Coalition's record, claiming they "did very little in their 10 years of government" on housing and voted against the Help to Buy scheme.

Coalition MPs were critical of the government's performance. One stated that "Australia is in the middle of the worst housing shortage in our nation's modern history," with rents soaring and home ownership "falling further and further out of reach" for young Australians. Another claimed that "just 44 per cent of Australians aged 25 to 34 own a home of their own," and that house prices have risen by "400 per cent over the last two decades." A different Coalition MP argued that "the focus should be on home affordability and ownership for younger Australians," but instead "older women are the fastest-growing group of homeless Australians—up to almost 40 per cent in a decade."

In the New South Wales Parliament, Opposition MP Eleni Petinos said her party would support the Help to Buy (Commonwealth Powers) Bill 2025, but criticised the Minns Labor Government for closing the state's Shared Equity Home Buyer scheme and for imposing a "$12,000 tax on new homes." In the Queensland Parliament, a government MP spoke in favour of the Revenue Legislation Amendment Bill 2024, which abolishes stamp duty on new homes for first home buyers and removes restrictions on renting out a room. In the Victorian Parliament, a government MP criticised the Opposition's stance on property tax, saying "a large portion of the property taxes are for developers to pay for the infrastructure for people and new communities."

sections.question: What positions have been taken on negative gearing and property tax concessions since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Government speakers have strongly defended reforms to negative gearing and capital gains tax (CGT) concessions. A government speaker said the bill "reforms negative gearing so that, from 1 July 2027, negative gearing for new residential property investment is focused on new builds," arguing tax concessions "should help add to the housing supply" rather than "encourage investors to compete with first home buyers for the same established homes." Another government speaker said they are "reforming negative gearing and capital gains tax concessions so that we level the playing field for first home buyers but grandfathering arrangements for some of the measures," adding that investors can still use negative gearing on new builds. A further government speaker stated they are "replacing the 50 per cent discount with cost-base indexation for gains accrued after 1 July, with a 30 per cent minimum tax." Senator Gallagher (Labor) said investment decisions made before budget night "are protected by the decisions we've made," resulting in "grandfathering arrangements for those who have investments that operated before budget night."

Opposition speakers have criticised the reforms. One said the government "attacked negative gearing and have gutted capital gains tax concessions—all while doing nothing about bracket creep," and claimed that "convinced that trusts are only used by billionaires, they planned wholesale changes that will cripple nearly 300,000 small businesses." Another opposition speaker claimed that "in the four years since coming to power, Labor has wasted $53 billion on tax concessions for wealthy property investors," asserting this "has actively contributed to pushing up house prices." A Greens speaker said the CGT discount and negative gearing "as currently designed, are worsening intergenerational inequity and doing nothing to solve the housing crisis," and called for reform of "other tax concessions that are overly generous to wealthy, older Australians." The record also includes a motion from Senator Bragg (Liberal) requesting Treasury advice on the impact of housing tax changes on supply and rents.

sections.question: What has parliament said about social and public housing supply since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Several speakers addressed social and public housing supply. In the New South Wales Parliament, Minister for Housing Rose Jackson reported that in 2023-24, the first year of the Minns Labor Government, "we completed 849 new homes. That is the largest number of homes delivered over the past decade," and that the government was on track to match that figure the following year. She contrasted this with the previous government's record, noting that under it "the policy was to sell public housing—over $3.6 billion was sold," and that completions dropped to "only 194 homes delivered in 2019-20." She also stated that the government had reduced the turnaround time for vacant public homes from 34.7 days in 2022-23 to 27.6 days, giving New South Wales "the fastest turnaround time for vacant homes in the country."

In the same parliament, Stephen Lawrence, a government member, said the Housing Amendment Bill 2025 supports the delivery of "8,400 new social homes and 21,000 new affordable and market homes as part of the Building Homes for NSW program," and that the government was "on track to deliver 850 new social homes" in the first year of that program. Minister Jackson also reported progress in regional New South Wales, stating that after delivering 416 regional homes in 2023-24 and 466 the following year, the state was "on track in 2025‑26 to deliver 749 homes in regional New South Wales." She noted that in Goulburn there were "55 homes in the pipeline."

At the Commonwealth level, a government speaker claimed that "More than 5,000 homes have already been completed with Commonwealth investment, with another 25,000 in planning or construction," and that the government was "delivering 5,000 social and affordable houses, with projects already underway in Tasmania," including more than 600 new social and affordable homes in that state through the Housing Australia Future Fund. However, an opposition senator in a Commonwealth estimates committee challenged the scale of delivery, stating that "around 190,000 households are currently on the public housing waitlist" while the government's plan supports "at most 55,000 households in new social and affordable homes and only for the next 25 years," arguing that "the scale of delivery does not match the scale of demand." The same committee heard a question about 4,935 unoccupied public and community housing dwellings as of 30 June 2024, while "nearly 42 per cent of greatest needs households have been waiting for more than two years for housing."

eras.label: 1993–2009
eras.question: How did parliament argue about housing between 1993 and 2009?
eras.answer:
Parliamentarians across the period debated housing affordability, public housing funding, and the tax treatment of low-income renters, often along partisan lines. A Labor speaker argued that tax expenditures on negative gearing exceeded spending on the Commonwealth-State Housing Agreement (CSHA), and cited the Industry Commission's 1993 finding "that the provision of public housing is a cost-effective way to meet government housing objectives." The same speaker claimed CSHA dwelling units fell from 372,134 in 1996 to 345,000 by 2003-04, and that new people receiving assistance dropped from 50,000 in 1996 to 25,000, with a projection of only 15,000 by 2009. Another Labor speaker criticised successive National Party community services ministers for rarely mentioning housing, alleging CSHA funding was cut by $100 million plus a further $360 million, and that 250,000 households were on public housing waiting lists. A different Labor speaker said the Howard government cut $200 million from public housing in the 1997-98 budget, and quoted a South Australian housing minister claiming GST effects would cut more than $100 million from public housing budgets.

A government speaker defended the Coalition's record, arguing "The most important thing you can do for housing affordability is to have low interest rates," noting rates were 6.55 per cent at the time compared with 10½ per cent in 1996 and 17 per cent in the late 1980s and early 1990s. That speaker also credited the First Home Owners Scheme with helping 387,000 Australians, and said the Commonwealth contributed $4 billion over four years to the CSHA while states provided only $1.4 billion. A later speaker, in 2009, announced a temporary boost: first home buyers purchasing a new home would receive a grant of $21,000, or $14,000 for an existing home, until 30 June 2009.

A recurring dispute concerned the GST on permanent residents of caravan parks and boarding houses. A Labor speaker said the government had promised rent would be GST-free, but instead these residents were classified as occupying "commercial residential premises" and faced a concessional rate that the speaker derided as "half of 10 equals 5.5." The speaker claimed a $33 million rent assistance increase reached only 3,955 of the 161,000 permanent caravan park residents, and quoted a constituent, Joan Armstrong, warning that "all such issues will not be forgotten at the next FEDERAL ELECTION." Another Labor speaker criticised the Democrats for voting for the GST and then attacking it, and said the government's national homelessness strategy pledged "no extra cent." On Indigenous housing, one speaker recounted a health worker saying the key to Indigenous children's health was "Improve the housing," while another speaker disputed any link between land control and housing provision, citing evidence from Professor Altman.

eras.label: 2010–2019
eras.question: How did parliament argue about housing between 2010 and 2019? The debates of the period included Residential Tenancies Amendment (Review) Bill 2018, Housing Affordability and Residential Tenancies Amendment (Social Housing) Bill 2018.
eras.answer:
The debates show deep division over how to handle social housing and tenancy law in New South Wales. The Government, through Minister Pru Goward, introduced the Residential Tenancies Amendment (Social Housing) Bill 2018 to target "the very small minority of tenants who do not value their property and the assistance this Government and the community provides." The bill mandated termination of tenancy for rental rebate fraud, introduced a risk-based rental bond scheme for tenants who cause significant damage, and gave community housing providers powers to terminate tenancies of registrable persons on police recommendation. Goward stressed that "the vast majority of good, responsible and law-abiding tenants" would be unaffected and that the changes would make the system "fairer and more equitable."

Opposition and crossbench members strongly criticised the bill. David Mehan (Labor) noted the Legislation Review Committee referred the bill to Parliament over concerns it "unduly trespasses on their right to housing," and argued the State was failing its housing responsibilities, pointing to a decline in social housing dwellings and rising homelessness. Justin Field (The Greens) said the party opposed the bill, calling it "punitive measures" at a time of high homelessness, and highlighted that a $1,400 bond could be "five times their weekly income" for a tenant on Newstart. Adam Searle (Labor) did not oppose the bill but moved amendments, arguing the "exceptional circumstances" test for avoiding termination was too narrow and that ministerial guidelines should be subject to parliamentary scrutiny rather than being an "absolute fiat" for the Minister. Tim Crakanthorp (Labor) raised concerns about retrospective bonds and the removal of tribunal discretion, while Melanie Gibbons (Liberal) supported the bill, saying good tenants were "sick and tired of having their communal spaces damaged."

Separately, debate on the Residential Tenancies Amendment (Review) Bill 2018 focused on private tenancy reform. Labor and The Greens pushed for an end to "no-grounds eviction," with David Mehan arguing that "all the benefits afforded by this bill... fall away without security of tenure." Jamie Parker (The Greens) supported parts of the bill, including domestic violence protections and minimum standards, but said much more was needed. Minister Matt Kean defended the bill as "commonsense reforms that strike a balance between the interests of tenants and the interests of landlords," and rejected claims the process had been too slow. The Commonwealth parliament also debated housing affordability, with one bill introducing a National Housing and Homelessness Agreement to replace the failed National Affordable Housing Agreement, and another creating an Automatic Rent Deduction Scheme for social housing tenants in arrears, described as a "preventative measure designed to stop the accrual of rental arrears, leading to eviction."

eras.label: 2020–2024
eras.question: How did parliament argue about housing between 2020 and the middle of 2024? The debates of the period included Public Housing, Affordable Housing and HomeBuilder Program.
eras.answer:
The parliamentary record shows sharp partisan conflict over housing policy, especially between the Coalition’s HomeBuilder program and the later Labor-led Housing Australia Future Fund. A government minister defended HomeBuilder, claiming it “has seen detached housing sales increase by 31 per cent” and loan approvals for new housing up by 20 per cent, supporting an industry employing up to one million people. In contrast, an opposition question cited Domain articles calling HomeBuilder “the most-complex least-equitable construction jobs program ever devised” and suggested renaming it “home blunder.” A Labor speaker also accused the Coalition of a “lost decade of minimal intervention and investment in social and affordable housing,” demanding to know where their housing investments were from 2013 to May 2022.

On the Housing Australia Future Fund Bill 2023, a Labor-aligned speaker described the package as “some of the most significant housing reforms we have seen in the last decade,” citing a $10 billion fund for social and affordable housing, including 20,000 social housing properties and 10,000 affordable homes for frontline workers over five years. The same speaker criticised the Greens and Liberals for “teaming up to oppose more investment in housing.” Another member, PENDER, said they were “pleased that the parliament will be doing more to support those who rely on affordable and social housing” but had “some concerns with the way the government is approaching this.” A Queensland Labor Treasurer was reported to have written to federal Labor’s housing minister asking for “a 12-month extension at the April 30, 2024 deadline for HomeBuilder.”

The record also includes state-level material. In South Australia, a committee report recommended the “Affordable Housing Initiative,” a five-year public sector program from late 2020 to 2025 delivering “1,000 new affordable home ownership opportunities” across metropolitan Adelaide and regional areas, self-funding with a projected surplus of $15.6 million and total expenditure of $407.3 million. A South Australian minister spoke of a partnership with builders and developers and referenced the state’s “Housing Future 2020:2030” strategy. A Commonwealth speaker noted that the federal government consulted on housing measures from 19 December 2022 to 11 January 2023, receiving 46 written submissions and holding three consultation sessions.

key_moments.title: Negative gearing and capital gains tax
key_moments.speaker: Andrew Leigh
key_moments.brief: Labor argued that negative gearing and capital gains tax discounts disproportionately benefit high-income earners, reduce home ownership, and cost the budget billions, proposing to halve the capital gains tax discount to 25% for new assets from July 2017 and grandfather existing investments. The speaker also criticised the government for scrapping Labor's permanent instant asset write-off and loss carry-back measures, and for failing to progress tax reform.
key_moments.why: Negative gearing and capital gains tax, Federal, 2016

key_moments.title: COVID-19 Rental Affordability
key_moments.speaker: R.A. Simms
key_moments.brief: The motion calls on the Marshall government to extend the eviction moratorium beyond 30 June, waive all COVID-19 rental debt, and introduce permanent rent caps, noting that no rental properties in South Australia are affordable for people on JobSeeker.

key_moments.title: Home Ownership
key_moments.speaker: Adam Crouch
key_moments.brief: Premier Dominic Perrottet announced the government's first home buyer choice policy, allowing buyers to opt for an annual land tax instead of upfront stamp duty, and noted over 13,000 people had used the online calculator, with Lakemba being the top electorate of interest.

key_moments.title: Housing Australia Future Fund Bill 2023
key_moments.speaker: Julie Collins
key_moments.brief: The government introduced the Housing Australia Future Fund bill, a $10 billion fund with annual disbursements capped at $500 million, intended to fund 30,000 social and affordable homes in its first five years. The bill also renames the National Housing Finance and Investment Corporation as Housing Australia and establishes the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council.
key_moments.why: Second reading, Housing Australia Future Fund Bill 2023, 2023

key_moments.title: Help To Buy (Commonwealth Powers) Bill
key_moments.speaker: Bolton
key_moments.brief: The speaker supported the bill to refer powers for the Help to Buy scheme, which would assist 40,000 participants nationally (2,000 in Queensland) through up to 40% Commonwealth shared equity, but noted criticisms from economist John Quiggin that subsidies are undesirable, the scheme has a lottery character, and social housing should be prioritised, while arguing the scheme is too small to address the housing crisis.
key_moments.why: Help To Buy (Commonwealth Powers) Bill, Queensland, 2024

key_moments.title: Housing
key_moments.speaker: Will Fowles
key_moments.brief: The speaker announced a broadcast housing crisis conversation with Major Brendan Nottle, Cr Sarah McKenzie and Rob Pradolin, arguing for urgent nonpartisan action and the Housing First principle to provide stable housing as the foundation for addressing homelessness.
